vignette:
Priya Nair is a 67-year-old South Asian American woman who has been married for over forty years and has spent the better part of her professional life coordinating outreach programs for a mid-sized non-profit focused on immigrant services in her city. She presented for psychological assessment several months after being sexually assaulted by a male acquaintance in her home, an event that shattered the sense of safety she had built carefully and quietly over decades.

The assault occurred on an afternoon when Priya had invited the man, a longtime peripheral figure in her community network, to discuss a potential collaboration for her organization. He arrived at her home while her husband was at a medical appointment. What followed was something Priya had, until that day, considered entirely outside the boundaries of her life. He forced himself on her in her own living room, in the early afternoon light, while the sounds of the neighborhood continued ordinarily outside. The ordinariness of everything around her - the hum of traffic, the familiar smell of her own home - became inseparable from what happened inside it.

In the weeks that followed, Priya found herself unable to give a coherent account of the assault, even to herself. When the memory surfaced, it did not arrive as a story with a beginning and an end; it arrived as fragments - the particular angle of afternoon light through the window, the weight of his hand, a sound she could not name but recognized completely. These pieces appeared without warning, pulled forward by things that had no obvious relationship to what had happened. A colleague entering her office and closing the door behind him was enough. The smell of a particular hand soap in the office restroom. The sound of a male voice lowering in conversation nearby. Each of these moments deposited her, without transition, back into that afternoon, and she would find herself gripping the edge of her desk or standing frozen in a hallway, certain, for those seconds, that she was not safe.

Priya had come to believe that something had been permanently altered in her - not only by the assault itself, but by her failure, as she understood it, to have prevented it or to have responded differently in the moment. She was certain that a woman of her age and experience should have known better than to be alone with him, should have read the signs, should have screamed or fought or done something that she had not done. This conviction sat at the center of her days like a stone. She told herself she was no longer the person her husband believed her to be, and this thought was among the most painful she carried.

She stopped attending the community meetings she had once organized with genuine investment. She routed her work increasingly through email rather than in-person contact and began scheduling site visits only when she could bring a younger female colleague along. Her team noticed that she had become less available, more formal in her manner, and one trusted coworker asked gently whether everything was all right. Priya said that she was tired. She had not told her husband what had happened. She had not told anyone. The silence had become its own structure, something she maintained with great effort and with the persistent fear that if she spoke, the version of herself that her family and colleagues had known for decades would become unrecognizable to them and to her.

Sleep had become unreliable. She woke frequently and lay in the dark beside her husband feeling profoundly alone. The world outside her window, which had once seemed largely benign, now seemed to her populated with potential repetitions of what had happened. She scanned faces at community events. She noticed where the exits were in rooms she had worked in for years.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a moment at work when she walked into a meeting room, saw a male colleague seated alone, and left without explanation. She stood in the corridor afterward and understood, with a clarity that frightened her, that she could not continue managing this alone. She came to the first session hoping, above everything else, to be believed - and afraid that what she would be asked to remember would be more than she could bear.
